abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
          <jats:p>Data sparseness is a major limiting factor for deep machine learning. In the natural sciences, data distributions are heterogeneous. For instance, in chemistry and early-phase drug discovery, compound and molecular property data are typically sparse compared to data in other fields such as particle physics or genome biology. For machine learning in low-data regimes, approaches such as transfer learning or meta-learning have been introduced. These learning strategies are conceptually related but algorithmically distinct and typically applied independently. They share the common goal of facilitating knowledge transfer between domains with related prediction tasks and varying data availability. We were interested in combining meta- and transfer learning into a coherent framework, primarily for deep learning in cheminformatics. Therefore, we introduce a new meta-learning algorithm designed to complement transfer learning. It identifies an optimal subset of training instances and determines weight initializations for deriving base models that can then be fine-tuned under conditions of data scarcity. Given its ability to identify preferred training samples, the meta-learning algorithm balances negative transfer between source and target domains, which represents a major caveat for transfer learning. In an extensive proof-of-concept application, inhibitors of protein kinases were predicted following data reduction using combined meta- and transfer learning, revealing statistically significant increases in model performance and effective control of negative transfer.</jats:p>

title: Machine Learning in Ligand-based Drug Design
abstract: <jats:p>The evolution of machine learning (ML) has fundamentally transformed ligand-based drug design (LBDD) by enabling the rapid identification, optimization, and prediction of bioactive compounds without reference to target structural information. This chapter investigates in great detail how different algorithms—from supervised ML models like random forests and support vector machines to deep learning and reinforcement learning frameworks—are used to examine vast chemical environments and predict ligand–target interactions in LBDD. Molecular representation strategies, including descriptors, fingerprints, and graph-based forms, are addressed here for the basis of developing predictive models. By presenting representative case studies, this chapter highlights successful ML-driven discoveries in many therapeutic domains, including COVID-19, diabetes, and cancer. It also discusses the shortcomings of current ML systems, including data scarcity, model interpretability, repeatability, and fit into current experimental techniques. To overcome the limitations, the chapter suggests increasing model transparency and clinical value by interdisciplinary collaboration, federated learning, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). The chapter concludes with a discussion on ethical frameworks and regulatory cooperation to guarantee the safe and efficient adoption of ML in the next drug discovery pipelines.</jats:p>
